title: perf-regression-canary-bisect-notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures our pragmatic runbook for investigating serving runtime performance regressions with a focus on canary comparisons, dashboards to check, and a bisect workflow to root-cause regressions quickly.

Scope / When to use:
- Use this when alerts fire for latency/throughput drops, GPU saturation anomalies, or when canary tests show divergence vs baseline.
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments (same observability surface).

Quick triage checklist (first 10-30 minutes):
1) Confirm alert details: alert name, threshold crossed, time window, affected regions/models.
2) Check canary vs baseline dashboard for the same time window. Is the regression seen only in canary or also in production?
3) Check traffic routing changes or recent rollout (PR/commit) that maps to the canary.
4) Determine blast radius: which customer tiers, model versions, regions are impacted?
5) If severity high (customer-facing / SLA), open an incident channel and consider immediate rollback of the canary.

Dashboards and metrics to inspect (priority order):
- Latency: p50, p95, p99, and tail percentiles for tokens and request latency (unit: ms). Compare canary vs baseline.
- Throughput: tokens/s and requests/s by model and route.
- GPU metrics: utilization, memory usage, encoder/decoder SM efficiency, PCIe bandwidth, GPU temperature.
- Host metrics: CPU utilization, syscall wait times, interrupts, cgroup throttling, IO wait.
- Queue/Backpressure: request queue length, queue wait time, batching size distribution.
- KV cache hit/miss rates and cache warmup curves (for decoder caching-sensitive models).
- Batching statistics: average batch size, batching latency, batch formation time.
- Worker pool metrics: worker restarts, OOMs, slow garbage collection (if using Python processes).
- External dependencies: storage/registry latency (model pull), KMS latency, networking errors (connection resets).

Checklist: Canary vs Baseline comparison:
- Time-align windows (use identical time slices, offset by timezone).
- Normalize for traffic: if canary has lower traffic, scale metrics or compare percentiles.
- Check model/version differences: exact model hash/weights and quantization profile.
- Compare hardware assignment: same instance types, GPU model, driver and CUDA versions.
- If canary config toggles exist (batching policy, kv-cache on/off, seq-len cap), ensure they're identical except the tested change.

Bisect process (finding the change that introduced the regression):
1) Scope candidates: list recent commits, PRs, infra changes, config flips, and model updates that landed before the regression window.
2) Create a minimal hypothesis set: code vs infra vs model vs config. For each hypothesis, identify a single variable to flip.
3) Automate binary search: use canary pipeline to roll forward/back between two revisions (A=known-good, B=current-bad). Run a deterministic micro-benchmark (short reproducible prompt set) on each revision and compare metrics.
4) Narrow by commits: if A and B are N commits apart, choose mid commit M and test A vs M and M vs B to narrow range.
5) If the regression is infra-related (driver/CUDA/AMI), prepare parallel environments with different drivers and run the same workload.
6) When candidate commit found, run additional profiling and add a short description to the bisect ticket.

Profiling and data collection steps (after initial triage):
- Capture perf traces (perf, py-spy/async-profiler) on CPU side for the serving process during the regression window.
- Capture GPU traces (nsys / nvprof) for encoder/decoder kernels and memcpy.
- Collect process-level sampling flamegraphs and native stack traces.
- Dump detailed request logs for a representative sample (include tokenization, batch id, latency breakdown per stage).
- Save exact model artifacts (weights, config) and runtime flags used for the test.
- Snapshot environment details: OS, kernel, driver, CUDA/cuDNN versions, container image digest, instance type.

Common root causes we repeatedly see:
- Batching regression: batch formation logic changed (longer formation time or smaller batch sizes) -> per-token cost increases.
- KV cache regressions: cache miss due to KV key encoding change or inadvertent cache flush.
- Kernel path changes: new kernel selection triggers slower kernels for common seq lengths.
- Memory layout/regression: quantization packing or allocator change causing more memcpy/overhead.
- External blocking: KMS or model pull latency causing head-of-line blocking.
- Regression in request routing: sticky routing sends high-latency hardware for some tenants.

Runbook for alerts (actions and communications):
- Severity P1 (customer-impacting): create incident, notify SRE + serving-runtime on-call, set status page if required. Immediate mitigation: rollback canary or route traffic away from impacted capacity.
- Severity P2: on-call investigates, gather traces and hypothesis, consider throttles or temporary config changes.
- Record timeline in the incident ticket and update stakeholders every 30-60 minutes until resolved.

Reproducing locally / smallest repro:
- Use the standard micro-benchmark script: tools/perf/run_repro.py --model <hash> --prompts <short-set> --batching-config <json> --seed 42
- Run with matching CUDA and driver in a dev GPU instance; use the exact container image digest.
- Instrument with the lightweight tracer (py-spy) first, then escalate to full nsys if needed.

Observability queries / snippets (PromQL examples, tweak to our metrics names):
- p95 latency for model X (canary): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(serving_request_latency_seconds_bucket{model="model-x",release="canary"}[5m])) by (le))
- avg batch size: sum(rate(serving_batch_sizes_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(serving_batch_sizes_count[5m]))
- KV cache hit rate: rate(kv_cache_hits_total[5m]) / (rate(kv_cache_hits_total[5m]) + rate(kv_cache_misses_total[5m]))

Notes / gotchas:
- Short regressions can be due to autoscaler churn; check recent scaling events and node replacements.
- Differences in load profiles (few large requests vs many small) can hide regressions if you only look at avg latency. Always include p95/p99.
- Canary pipeline noise: ensure the canary test harness warms the KV cache and primes model weights to avoid cold-start noise.

Postmortem / follow-up actions (if regression validated):
- Add test coverage: unit/regression benchmark into perf CI gated by PRs touching critical paths.
- Add a canary metric for the specific root cause (e.g., batch formation time, kernel swap count).
- Retro item: evaluate if the rollout strategy needs stricter guards (more traffic ramp, longer canaries, forced warm-up).

Open action items / TODOs:
- [ ] Add automated bisect job in CI to run perf micro-benchmarks across commit ranges (Ravi).
- [ ] Create a dashboard widget that highlights per-model kernel selection distribution (Li).
- [ ] Add a canary warm-up step to the deployment pipeline (SRE + runtime).
- [ ] Document exact repro prompt set and store under tools/repro/prompt_sets/canary_repro.txt (Marta).

Questions / unresolved:
- Do we want bisect results written as annotations into the Prometheus timeseries (so we can visualize commit boundaries)? Pros/cons?
- Should we standardize on a single profiling stack (nsys + py-spy) and provide reproducible instructions in the developer guide?

Appendix: quick links and references:
- Bisect script: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tools/bisect_helper (example usage in PR #987)
- Canary dashboard: dashboards/serving-runtime/canary-comparison
- Incident playbook (triage): https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/PRF-TRIAGE

(Working draft - save iterations here. Keep notes brief and actionable. If you add new telemetry, append the metric name to the top of this doc.)
